title: 14-year-old with brief, frequent attacks of incoordination triggered by sudden movement

provenance.citation: Synthetic case drafted 2026-10-17 for Rare Disease Detective; not derived from any individual patient.

chief_complaint: "When I suddenly start running or get startled, my legs and hands go wobbly for a minute."
history_of_present_illness: Since age 9, brief attacks lasting 30 seconds to 3 minutes of limb incoordination, unsteadiness and slurred speech, up to 10–15 times on bad days and none on others. Triggered by sudden movement (standing up quickly, starting a sprint), startle, emotional upset, and occasionally by kicking a ball hard. Attacks are more frequent when she is ill or has had a poor night's sleep. During attacks she feels 'drunk': she cannot walk in a straight line, her hands miss what she reaches for, and friends say her words 'run together'. She does not describe twisting or jerking of the limbs, though she sometimes feels her hands 'stiffen' briefly afterwards. Sometimes she feels the muscles of her hands and around her eyes 'ripple' between attacks, like 'worms under the skin'. No loss of consciousness, no tongue biting, no incontinence, no post-attack confusion. No vertigo, headache, or double vision with attacks. Normal between attacks except for occasional calf and hand stiffness after exercise. Development and school performance are normal.

symptom_timeline.event: Pediatrician notes attacks provoked by sudden movement; raises a paroxysmal dyskinesia
EEG and MRI brain normal; seizures considered unlikely
Frequency increases with puberty and competitive soccer
Attacks interfere with soccer and PE; referred to movement-disorder clinic

movement_findings.observation: Attack provoked in clinic by rising quickly from a squat: 90-second episode of bilateral limb ataxia with dysmetria on finger–nose, wide-based unsteady gait, and slurred dysarthric speech; no dystonic or choreic postures; fully responsive throughout.
Interictal: fine continuous rippling of periorbital muscles and small hand muscles (first dorsal interosseous), consistent with myokymia; more visible after the provoked attack.
Interictal: no nystagmus in primary gaze, lateral gaze, or after head-shaking.
Immediately after the provoked attack: brief stiffness of the hands with slightly slow finger opening, resolving within a minute.

neurological_exam.other: Hand muscle myokymia visible. No percussion myotonia; grip release normal at rest. Sensation normal.

neurophysiology.report: Normal awake and asleep. No attack captured. Hyperventilation and photic stimulation unremarkable.

family_history: Father (44) had similar 'wobbly spells' as a teenager, triggered by running, that diminished in his 20s; never investigated. Paternal grandfather described as 'clumsy'. Mother and younger brother (10) healthy. No family history of epilepsy or migraine. No consanguinity.
social_history: Year 9 student, good grades. Plays competitive soccer 3 times a week; has stopped playing as a striker because sprint starts trigger attacks. No alcohol, smoking, or drugs. No regular medications.
prior_workup_and_opinions: Pediatrician (age 10): raised paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia because attacks are triggered by sudden movement; no treatment trial undertaken. Pediatric neurology (age 11): EEG and MRI normal, 'not epileptic'.
